Substack CEO Chris Best framed the tool as a transparency measure against what he calls "Claudefishing" — when readers unknowingly engage with content that has no genuine human thought behind it. Writers can also scan their own drafts, add a "How I make this" statement, and report inaccurate detection results.
quote: "Platforms that reward fakeness will create a race to the bottom." — Chris Best, Cofounder and CEO, Substack

title: Evals are the new PRD, Expedia’s AI chief tells VB Transform 2026
summary: Expedia Group's chief AI and data officer Xavi Amatriain argued at VB Transform 2026 that evaluation frameworks — not traditional product requirement documents — should define what AI products do, with all design thinking encoded into evals before coding begins. He warned that excessive guardrails are counterproductive, distorting user feedback loops and making systems more brittle, and instead advocated for risk-calibrated governance through layered principles, processes, and automated toll gates tied to each agent's risk level. Amatriain also outlined Expedia's architecture of specialized, composable agents rather than monolithic AI, and stated that users must retain the final booking action as a non-negotiable security design principle. VentureBeat survey data underscored the stakes: 54% of enterprises have already experienced an agent security incident or near-miss, while only 5% fully trust the automated evaluations underpinning production deployments.
quote: "You're gonna get threats coming not only from humans but also from other external agentic systems that are really powerful, and they're gonna be poking at everything you're doing." — Xavi Amatriain, Chief AI and Data Officer, Expedia Group

title: Data centers expected to use 4x more electricity by 2035
summary: A new BloombergNEF report projects U.S. data centers will consume one-fifth of all domestically generated electricity by 2035, four times current levels, driven largely by surging AI compute demand. Total data center capacity is expected to reach nearly 200 gigawatts, with nearly half dedicated to AI training and inference, and the U.S. hosting 64% of AI chips by power demand by 2033. The forecast is 83% higher than BloombergNEF's own December estimate, reflecting rapid upward revisions across the industry — EPRI more than doubled its 2024 estimate and S&P's forecast rose by over a third in six months. The strain is already visible in key grid regions: electricity prices in PJM, which spans Virginia to Illinois, have risen 76% over the past year, and one major utility has threatened to exit the interconnection entirely.

title: Anthropic’s $1.5B copyright settlement approved; only 350 authors opted out
summary: A US federal judge approved a $1.5 billion settlement between Anthropic and authors on Monday, ending the largest copyright class-action ever certified against an AI company. The case had established that Anthropic's AI training on books constituted fair use, but that its piracy of works likely did not. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín reduced lawyers' fees from the requested 12.5 percent to under 7 percent of the settlement fund (roughly $101 million), while approving per-work payouts of approximately $3,000 — four times the minimum statutory damages. With 91 percent of affected authors and publishers already filing claims and only 350 opting out, the settlement signals broad acceptance of AI training fair-use precedent while requiring Anthropic to destroy all covered works.
quote: "We are pleased that more than 91 percent of authors and publishers covered by the settlement have claimed their share of the payment, and we're looking forward to bringing this matter to a close." — Aparna Sridhar, Deputy General Counsel, Anthropic

title: Google releases three new Gemini models — but no 3.5 Pro
summary: Google DeepMind released three new Gemini models — Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, and 3.5 Flash Cyber — focused on efficiency, lower cost, and cybersecurity, with the latter exclusively available to governments and trusted partners. The launches are notable for what was absent: the long-anticipated Gemini 3.5 Pro, Google's flagship model, which has not been updated since February while rivals OpenAI and Anthropic have continued rapid releases. Bloomberg previously reported internal delays tied to unmet performance goals. Google DeepMind's Logan Kilpatrick confirmed the company is testing 3.5 Pro with partners and has begun its "most ambitious pre-training run yet" for Gemini 4, signaling continued investment in frontier capabilities even as the near-term flagship update remains elusive.
quote: "We are currently testing Gemini 3.5 Pro with partners and hopes to land soon." — Logan Kilpatrick, Google DeepMind product lead

title: Google announces Gemini 3.6 Flash and cybersecurity AI, teases 3.5 Pro and Gemini 4
summary: Google has released Gemini 3.6 Flash, replacing 3.5 Flash, along with a new Flash Lite model and a cybersecurity-focused Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, while confirming it has begun pre-training for Gemini 4. The 3.6 Flash model improves on coding benchmarks and reduces token usage by about 17 percent, with a slightly lower output cost of $7.50 per million tokens versus $9 for its predecessor. The cybersecurity model, deemed too sensitive for public release, will launch as a limited pilot through Google DeepMind's CodeMender agent for trusted partners and governments only. Google also confirmed that the long-delayed Gemini 3.5 Pro — intended to rival GPT 5.6 and Claude Fable/Sonnet 5 — is still in partner testing with no firm release date.

title: Anthropic’s $1.5 billion book piracy settlement approved by judge
summary: A federal judge has approved Anthropic's $1.5 billion class action settlement with authors who accused the company of training its AI models on pirated books, with authors receiving approximately $3,000 per book. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín signed off on the deal Monday, calling it "meaningful relief" and noting it represents the largest known copyright recovery in history. Over 91% of eligible authors and publishers have claimed their share of the payment. Anthropic still faces additional copyright lawsuits from other authors who argue the per-book payment is insufficient.
quote: "We are pleased that more than 91% of authors and publishers covered by the settlement have claimed their share of the payment." — Aparna Sridhar, Anthropic General Counsel

title: US threatens sanctions against Chinese AI models over IP theft
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Tuesday that the U.S. will examine Chinese open-source AI models for signs of intellectual property theft and may impose sanctions on Chinese AI companies if theft is established. The move comes as Chinese models like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 gain capabilities and popularity, threatening the business models and fundraising prospects of American AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. The administration is also reportedly considering a wholesale ban on Chinese open-source models, marking a potential significant escalation beyond existing chip export controls. The policy debate is complicated by industry disagreement over whether model distillation — a key technique Chinese developers are accused of using — actually constitutes theft, with critics noting it is widely practiced by U.S. companies as well.
quote: "If we see, especially, that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them because of this theft." — Scott Bessent, Treasury Secretary

title: Google launches a cheaper alternative to large AI security models like Mythos
summary: Google has launched Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, a cost-efficient cybersecurity AI model designed to find and patch software vulnerabilities faster and more cheaply than larger competing systems such as Anthropic's Mythos. Built on Gemini 3.5 Flash, the model is being made available first to governments and trusted partners through CodeMender, Google's security-focused coding agent, which can invoke the model multiple times at high speed to scan more code paths. On a key cybersecurity benchmark, the model identified 55 unique confirmed issues in the V8 JavaScript Engine — outperforming Gemini 3.5 Flash (47) and Anthropic's Opus 4.6 (36), including 10 issues no other model found. The launch signals an accelerating competitive race in AI-powered cybersecurity, with Google positioning smaller, cheaper models as viable alternatives to compute-heavy offerings like Mythos, which costs twice as much as Claude Opus 4.8.

title: Music streamer Deezer says more than 50% of daily uploads are AI-generated
summary: Deezer revealed that AI-generated tracks now account for more than 50% of daily uploads to its platform, peaking at 90,000 tracks per day in June 2026. This is a dramatic rise from 10,000 tracks per day (10% of uploads) in January 2025. In response, Deezer will remove AI-generated tracks that have gone unstreamed for six months or are linked to fraudulent streaming activity. The development highlights a growing industry challenge, with streaming platforms diverging sharply on how to handle AI music — from Bandcamp's outright ban and Tidal's monetization cutoff to Apple Music's voluntary tagging and Spotify's usage-based policy.
quote: "Now that half of all daily uploads are AI-generated tracks, we are taking additional steps to safeguard the rights of artists and songwriters, while maintaining focus on music that fans actually love." — Alexis Lanternier, CEO, Deezer

title: Tailscale catches AI tailwinds as it nears 40,000 paid business customers
summary: Canadian networking startup Tailscale is approaching 40,000 paid business customers — double its count from November 2025 — driven largely by AI adoption, including AI agents that have begun autonomously recommending, purchasing, and deploying its VPN software. CEO Avery Pennarun credits a significant inflection point to the rise of OpenClaw, a widely adopted open-source AI agent, whose users have shown unexpectedly high retention on Tailscale's platform. The company, which counts Cohere, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Mistral among its clients, reports 100% year-over-year growth in private network creation and now has two million monthly active users. Tailscale is also weighing a new funding round to accelerate growth, having already closed a $230-million CAD Series C at a $2-billion valuation, and says it could reach profitability within a year on its existing balance sheet.
quote: "Tailscale is, almost by accident, the tool of choice for a lot of AIs and AI agents that are running around now." — Avery Pennarun, Co-founder and CEO

title: America needs to stop getting shocked by Chinese AI
summary: Two new Chinese AI models — Kimi K3 from Moonshot AI and Qwen3.8 from Alibaba — have launched with performance claims rivaling top US systems from OpenAI and Anthropic, at significantly lower prices, yet again triggering market turbulence and "Sputnik moment" comparisons. The article argues the real surprise is that these releases are still being treated as surprises, given that Chinese labs have been visibly closing the gap for years, with six of the top 10 AI tools by usage on OpenRouter's leaderboard already Chinese. Both models are planned as open-weight releases, a sharp contrast to the closed approach of leading US labs, which could accelerate adoption and further pressure US companies' market positions and anticipated trillion-dollar IPO valuations. The piece warns that whether Chinese models rank in the top five or top ten globally matters less than the strategic reality: China is now producing frontier-competitive AI with enough regularity that each release should no longer be treated as a shock.
quote: "If this really is a race, it's time to accept that someone else might actually win, or at least get close enough that they might as well have." — Robert Hart, AI Reporter

title: Gritt exits stealth with $32 million for robots to build solar plants — then, everything else
summary: Gritt, a robotics startup founded by two Carnegie Mellon-trained roboticists, has emerged from stealth with $32 million in total funding, including a $26 million Series A led by Obvious Ventures, to deploy AI-powered robotic systems that dramatically accelerate solar panel installation. The company's systems — built on off-the-shelf hardware controlled by its proprietary AI models — allow an eight-person crew to install 3,000 to 4,000 panels per day, compared to 800 without the technology. Gritt is contracted to help install 2.8 gigawatts of solar panels over the next 18 months, with customers including three of the top 10 U.S. power construction companies. The startup's broader ambition is to use the same generalizable AI pipeline to expand into other labor-intensive construction tasks, positioning its systems as an on-site intelligence layer for decision-making beyond physical installation.
quote: "Our thesis is that if we truly want to speed up construction, you need an intelligence which can work in the outdoor, chaotic environments of these construction sites, and it has to be generalizable enough that it can work in these varied environments." — Puneet Puri, CEO

title: Anthropic’s landmark $1.5B copyright settlement is approved
summary: A federal judge has granted final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement with authors and book publishers, resolving a class action lawsuit over the AI company's use of copyrighted works to train its models. The settlement, believed to be the largest in U.S. copyright history, will pay approximately $3,000 per work across an estimated 500,000 titles. Critically, the presiding judge had ruled that training AI on copyrighted text constitutes fair use — a significant win for the AI industry — but found that Anthropic's use of pirate sites such as Library Genesis to obtain books was itself illegal, prompting the settlement to avoid a jury trial on damages. Because Anthropic settled before an appeal, the fair use ruling remains a single district court decision and does not set binding precedent, leaving the broader legal question open as copyright suits against Google, Meta, Midjourney, and OpenAI continue.

title: Trump’s latest AI czar has already resigned
summary: Chris Fall, director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), has resigned just three months after being appointed, making him the second person to leave the role in rapid succession in 2026. His predecessor, Collin Burns, departed in under a week in April, reportedly pushed out due to his prior work at Anthropic amid the administration's tensions with the company. CAISI, which operates under NIST and is responsible for developing AI technical standards and testing methods, appears to be losing influence — it was notably absent from the recently signed Gold Eagle executive order on AI safety oversight. The instability comes as the administration weighs banning Chinese open-source AI models and Google DeepMind's CEO calls for an industry-run standards body to fill precisely the role CAISI was created for.

title: Here are the 30,000 songs Sony is suing Udio’s AI music generator over
summary: Sony Music Entertainment has filed a new lawsuit against AI music generator Udio in a New York court, alleging copyright infringement of more than 30,000 songs, including works by Elvis Presley, Beyoncé, Britney Spears, and Harry Styles. Sony says the list represents only a small portion of works Udio infringed, and was identified through "audio fingerprinting" of Udio's training data obtained through discovery. A judge previously rejected Sony's attempt to expand its original 2024 lawsuit — which covered 333 works — to include these additional songs, prompting the new filing. Sony is seeking up to $150,000 per infringed work and a block on further infringement, while co-plaintiffs Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group have already settled with Udio and entered licensing partnerships with the company.

title: Google is working on a new AI chip designed to make Gemini more efficient
summary: Google is developing a new server chip internally called "Frozen v2," slated for release in 2028, that could be six to ten times more efficient than its existing AI chips, measured by tokens generated per unit of power. The chip is designed to improve the efficiency of Google's Gemini models and reduce dependence on Nvidia, which has historically dominated the AI chip market. The news follows similar moves by OpenAI, which announced its first custom inference chip dubbed "Jalapeño," and Anthropic, which is reportedly in talks with Samsung on a chipmaking partnership. Investor reaction was positive, with Alphabet's stock climbing roughly 3% following the report, a meaningful signal as the company faces scrutiny over its planned $180–$190 billion AI spending commitment.

title: SpaceX in your index fund, explained
summary: SpaceX's fast-tracked entry into the Nasdaq-100 — enabled by a rule change the company itself requested — means index fund investors now hold shares in a stock that governance experts and some economists consider overpriced and uniquely risky due to Elon Musk's near-total control. The company entered the index on July 7, 2026, with its weighting initially constrained because fewer than 5% of shares were sold in the IPO, but that will grow as employee lockup periods expire, with a major release expected after SpaceX publishes Q2 results in mid-August. Burton Malkiel, a foundational architect of index fund theory, argues investors should not abandon index funds over SpaceX, because only about 4% of stocks drive long-term market returns and no expert can reliably identify them in advance. The article also notes SpaceX's IPO sets a precedent for other expected mega-IPOs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, which are anticipated later in 2026.
quote: "A very small minority of stocks are responsible for the whole return, and experts can't pick them any better than the index as a whole." — Burton Malkiel, Economist and Index Fund Pioneer

title: OpenAI is scared of open-weight models. Should the US be?
summary: OpenAI's head of strategic futures publicly argued that the US government should manufacture regulatory uncertainty around open-weight AI models — particularly China's Kimi K3 from Moonshot — to protect frontier labs' capital investments, before retracting those claims after significant backlash. The Trump administration is reportedly considering banning K3 and other advanced Chinese models at the behest of American frontier labs, though the Department of Commerce has signaled it won't act soon. The core tension is economic: capable open-weight models offer cheaper AI than closed-lab offerings, threatening the margins of companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, but experts argue that restricting them would cede innovation leadership to China and concentrate AI power dangerously. Chip export controls, not open-model bans, are seen by some analysts as a more effective and less market-distorting way to preserve US AI leadership.
quote: "The main point is the U.S. would be very well served to have its own very capable, much less expensive open models. It just clashes with the approach the frontier labs have taken." — Sam Bresnick, China-focused research fellow, Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology

title: China’s AI models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself
summary: Moonshot's Kimi, a free open-source AI model from China that rivals the capabilities of paid models from OpenAI and Anthropic, has exposed deep divisions among Trump administration AI advisors over how to respond to Chinese AI competition. The model's release triggered a public dispute between current and former officials, with ex-AI czar David Sacks criticizing top US AI companies for seeking government protection against open-source competition, while Pentagon official Emil Michael attacked those favoring a hands-off approach. The disagreement reflects a broader strategic split: one faction sees open AI development as beneficial, while another wants government intervention to vet and control frontier AI releases on national security grounds. The episode highlights a growing economic and political problem for the Trump administration, as capable free Chinese models undercut the business models of US AI companies that are driving significant stock market and economic activity.

title: Adobe’s ‘natural look’ camera app embraces generative AI
summary: Adobe's experimental iPhone camera app, Project Indigo, has added a suite of generative AI editing tools called "AI Playground" in its version 1.1 update, marking a significant shift from its original pitch as a natural, SLR-like photography experience. The new features include AI-generated style filters, object removal with generative fill, photo feedback via AI analysis, and a custom prompting tool — powered by Google's Nano Banana AI model rather than Adobe's own Firefly. The update is being tested with a small percentage of users, with a paid version possible if the experiment proves popular. Notably, Adobe has not yet implemented its usual C2PA Content Credentials transparency standard for AI-edited images produced through Indigo, though Google's invisible SynthID watermark is applied.
quote: "This is the beginning of a journey for Adobe — towards an integrated mobile camera and editing experience that takes advantage of the latest advances in computational photography and AI." — Marc Levoy, Adobe Fellow

title: Safety guardrails blocked Hugging Face's defenders, not the attacker, when an AI agent breached its systems
summary: An autonomous AI agent breached Hugging Face's production infrastructure over a weekend in July 2026, harvesting cloud and cluster credentials after exploiting two code-execution paths in a malicious dataset ingested by the company's data pipeline. When Hugging Face's incident response team turned to commercial frontier AI models to analyze the attack, safety guardrails blocked their forensic queries — treating real exploit data the same way they would treat a live attack — while the attacker's agent operated under no such restrictions. The forensic investigation ultimately ran on GLM 5.2, an open-weight model deployed on Hugging Face's own infrastructure, keeping sensitive attack data inside the company's environment. The incident exposes a structural gap: commercial AI safety systems have no way to distinguish an authenticated incident responder from a malicious actor, making those tools unreliable precisely when defenders need them most.
quote: "The attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried." — Hugging Face, Disclosure Statement

title: YouTube clarifies policies around AI slop and upsetting videos
summary: YouTube has updated its YouTube Partner Program (YPP) monetization policies to more precisely define what counts as "inauthentic content" ineligible for revenue sharing. The revised rules, effective July 16, 2026, break the category into three types: generic or repetitive AI- and template-generated videos, off-putting or emotionally manipulative content designed to chase views, and AI personas used to discuss sensitive topics such as health, finance, or legal matters. The move is aimed at curbing "content farming" — channels that exploit AI tools to mass-produce low-quality videos purely for ad revenue — while preserving monetization for creators who use AI to enhance genuinely original work. The policy shift carries financial stakes for Google, as YouTube now generates more ad revenue than rival streamers and has surpassed Netflix in average daily views worldwide.
quote: "The same technology really enables great stuff, but it also enables stuff that's kind of content farming, and that's the stuff that we don't want to have in YPP." — Matt Halprin, Trust and Safety Chief, YouTube

title: Personal training app Flex AI is shutting down
summary: Canadian AI-powered fitness startup Flex AI, based in Vancouver, shut down operations in March 2026 after exhausting its funding and failing to secure an acquisition, CEO Amin Niri confirmed. The company, founded in 2018, had developed on-device computer vision technology for real-time exercise form feedback and reached nearly one million users at its peak. Niri acknowledged that some markets are "almost impossible to win in, economically," pointing to the intense crowding in the health and fitness app space, where high market saturation and user retention remain major challenges despite the sector generating $3.4 billion in annual revenue globally. The shutdown was complicated by unpaid contractors, though Niri said he has since resolved those obligations, drawing on personal family loans where company funds were insufficient.
quote: "Winding down a company I spent seven years building, and doing right by the people who built it with me, has been the hardest thing I've done professionally." — Amin Niri, Co-founder and CEO, Flex AI

title: China delivers a one-two punch to America’s AI dominance
summary: Moonshot AI and Alibaba have unveiled new frontier AI models — Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8 — that their creators claim rival the best systems from OpenAI and Anthropic, intensifying the US-China AI race. Both Chinese models are being released as open-weight systems, allowing developers worldwide to freely download and adapt them, a sharp contrast to the proprietary approach of leading US labs. Moonshot's Kimi K3, described as the world's largest open-source AI model at 2.8 trillion parameters, is set for full release on July 27th, while Alibaba's 2.4 trillion parameter Qwen3.8 is also expected to go open-weight soon. The releases raise fresh questions about whether massive US investment in chips and data centers can sustain a durable lead if Chinese rivals can match the frontier at lower cost — echoing the disruption caused by DeepSeek's emergence last year.

title: An Indigenous AI framework
summary: At Mila's Indigenous AI Gathering in Montréal, Canadian AI minister Evan Solomon and Indigenous researchers outlined an alternative vision for AI development that centers Indigenous communities rather than leaving them behind. The gathering showcased smaller, open-source AI models with lower energy footprints designed to advance Indigenous economic interests, offering a contrast to the federal government's focus on speed and global competitiveness. The event highlighted ongoing tensions between Canada's push to accelerate AI infrastructure — including data centres — and Indigenous data sovereignty concerns, compounded by a history of government exploitation of Indigenous data. Whether Ottawa will incorporate these principles into concrete policy remains uncertain, as the government has yet to detail how it will weigh environmental priorities or ensure Indigenous data sovereignty.
quote: "I see this technological revolution coming, and there's a lot of Indigenous people who are being left behind." — Mick Elliott, Mila Research Fellow, Okanese First Nation

title: AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring
summary: New research from Princeton University and the University of Chicago finds that leading LLMs — including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini — stereotype job candidates by demographic group more aggressively than humans do, and can develop entirely novel biases from experience rather than just inheriting them from training data. In simulated hiring experiments, models scored roughly 65% higher than human participants on a segregation scale, with OpenAI's o3 model approaching the maximum possible score. Stronger reasoning models, including o3 and DeepSeek's R1, showed even more pronounced bias, because their optimization for generalizing from limited data accelerates stereotyping in social contexts. The findings carry direct implications for companies deploying AI to screen résumés or conduct interviews, particularly as chatbots gain persistent memory features that could compound bias over time.
quote: "These novel biases—they're sort of ever present." — Ryan Liu, PhD student, Princeton University

title: What to watch for after Jensen Huang’s Japan visit
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's two-day Tokyo visit in July 2026 produced deals spanning Japan's entire tech ecosystem, centered on physical AI for factory floors and robotics. Japan's government-backed consortium Noetra — anchored by SoftBank, Sony, NEC, and Honda — will oversee an Nvidia-powered AI factory housing 13,750 Vera CPUs and 27,500 Rubin GPUs, backed by up to 1 trillion yen ($6.2 billion) over five years. Major Japanese robotics and manufacturing firms including Fanuc, Yaskawa, Toyota, Kawasaki Heavy, and Fujitsu are committing to build on Nvidia's Cosmos models, with Japan targeting 10 million AI-equipped robots across 18 sectors by 2040. The broader strategic ambition is sovereign AI infrastructure: Japan wants its own data, compute, and foundation models — though for now, that independence runs on American chips.
quote: "The next frontier of AI is in the physical world, and this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Japan." — Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia

title: Can an Apple lawsuit derail OpenAI’s hardware plans?
summary: Apple filed a trade secrets lawsuit against OpenAI in July 2026, accusing the AI company of systematically recruiting current and former Apple employees to extract confidential information, with OpenAI's chief hardware officer Tang Tan named in the complaint. The lawsuit arrives at a critical moment for OpenAI, which is reportedly developing its first hardware product — a screenless mobile smart speaker — and has confidentially filed for an IPO expected as early as late 2026 or early 2027. Analysts and reporters at TechCrunch's Equity podcast note the lawsuit could delay OpenAI's hardware development, complicate its IPO pricing if hardware revenue projections are clouded by legal risk, and force the company to fight on multiple fronts simultaneously. OpenAI denied awareness of any evidence supporting the complaint, and TechCrunch's Kirsten Korosec predicts OpenAI will fight rather than settle, drawing on confidence gained from its recent courtroom win against Elon Musk.
quote: "They don't do this stuff willy nilly." — Sean O'Kane, Reporter, TechCrunch

title: ‘Odyssey’ director Christopher Nolan calls AI an obvious ‘Trojan horse’
summary: Christopher Nolan, director of the new blockbuster "The Odyssey" and president of the Directors Guild of America, has publicly described AI as a "transparent horse, it's made of glass" — a Trojan horse whose dangers are already obvious to the public. Nolan noted he has "never seen a technology advancing so rapidly so completely rejected by the public," citing young people's swift dismissal of AI-generated content as "AI slop" as a sign of healthy skepticism. He argued that both the technology and the motives of those promoting it must be viewed critically rather than accepted on blind faith. His comments carry institutional weight given his DGA leadership role, which recently secured generative AI protections in the guild's latest contract.

title: Nonprofit Current AI is racing to build the World Wide Web of AI, free for all
summary: Current AI, a nonprofit founded in February 2025 and seeded with $100 million from the French government plus contributions from Ford Foundation, MacArthur Foundation, DeepMind, and Salesforce — totaling $400 million committed — is building open, public AI infrastructure as an alternative to privately owned AI systems. The organization has deployed $3.2 million in grants to projects in Kenya, Lebanon, and the Brazilian Amazon focused on underrepresented languages and community-controlled data, and last week launched Alpha Chat, an open-source chatbot built in seven weeks by a coalition including Hugging Face, Mozilla, and MIT Media Lab. CEO Ayah Bdeir frames the mission as a direct challenge to Big Tech's dominance: if AI will transform every aspect of life, a public alternative modeled on the open web must exist. The initiative signals a growing institutional push — backed by governments and major philanthropies — to create AI infrastructure outside the commercial model.
quote: "If AI is truly a transformative technology, if it's going to change every aspect of everyone's life, there has to be a public alternative." — Ayah Bdeir, CEO, Current AI

title: Dave Eggers told OpenAI staff that ChatGPT was ‘silencing an entire generation’
summary: Author Dave Eggers used an invitation from Sam Altman to address roughly 200 OpenAI employees as an opportunity to criticize the company's impact on education and writing. Eggers argued that ChatGPT has made teachers' lives significantly harder and that students who use it to compose written work will never develop their own voice or writing ability. He framed this as a generational harm, warning that an entire generation could be silenced by losing the capacity to express their own truth. Altman likely anticipated a critical reception given Eggers' history — his novel The Circle is a well-known critique of the tech industry, and he has previously dismissed AI-generated writing as "pastiche nonsense."
quote: "If students are using it to compose, which is the biggest tragedy of all, they'll never learn to write. And their voice is stolen from them." — Dave Eggers, Author

title: Kimi: Threat or menace?
summary: Moonshot AI's release of Kimi K3, an open-source model that independent evaluations show is competitive with leading frontier models like Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, has reignited debate over China's AI competitiveness — echoing but intensifying the reaction to DeepSeek's R1 release in January 2025. The announcement coincided with Xi Jinping's speech at the World AI Conference in Shanghai and rattled markets, with the Nasdaq falling roughly 1% as chip stocks sold off. Responses from U.S. tech and policy figures ranged from warnings about regulatory self-sabotage (David Sacks) to suggestions that the Trump administration should manufacture regulatory uncertainty around Chinese open-weight models without needing to formally ban them (Dean Ball). The episode highlights deepening tensions over open-source AI, U.S.-China competition, and whether frontier-capable open models ultimately serve American strategic interests.
quote: "You just need to direct every agency to issue soft law that creates FUD. 'A Federal Reserve Advisory Bulletin found that there may be backdoors in Chinese AI models.' It needn't be that well justified. You just create enough regulatory risk that every regulated enterprise backs off." — Dean Ball, Head of Strategic Futures, OpenAI

title: Will AI fix prior authorization—or make it worse?
summary: The Trump administration is piloting a program called WISeR (Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction Model) across six states, using AI and machine learning to reduce unnecessary spending in original Medicare through prior authorization — a system rarely used in original Medicare before. Critics warn the model has already caused care delays and wrongful denials, and that vendors earn a share of "averted expenditures," creating financial incentives to reject care. Meanwhile, a Commonwealth Fund survey found roughly one in five working-age Americans with private insurance were denied coverage for physician-recommended care in 2025, with over a quarter reporting their health worsened as a result. The administration is simultaneously pressuring private insurers to reduce prior authorization burdens, creating a contradictory posture that has drawn significant political and medical community pushback.
quote: "AI should be used to make appropriate care easier to approve, not necessary care easier to deny." — Camm Epstein, Health Policy Analyst

title: Vertu wants executives to pay $6,880 for an AI agent — a performance review
summary: Vertu's Alphafold, a $6,880 luxury foldable phone built on ZTE Nubia hardware, centers its pitch on Hermes Agent, an AI designed to automate executive workflows including document analysis, travel planning, and multi-step task execution. In hands-on testing by TechCrunch, Hermes showed greater autonomy than Samsung's Gemini on the Galaxy Z Fold 7, often attempting entire multi-step workflows without asking for clarification, but produced notable errors including a wrong-time reminder, incorrect calendar dates, and lost document context between sessions. Gemini, by contrast, asked clarifying questions before acting and retained conversation context reliably, ultimately delivering more accurate outcomes despite completing fewer steps autonomously. The review concludes that Hermes Agent is ambitious but inconsistent, positioning the Alphafold as a luxury status symbol with a promising but unfinished AI layer rather than a proven executive productivity tool.

title: Databricks hits $188B valuation, extending its run as AI’s favorite second act
summary: Databricks announced a new funding round valuing the company at $188 billion, led by Coatue, with approximately $3 billion expected to close later in summer 2026. The raise marks the latest in a rapid valuation climb — from $62 billion in December 2024 to $100 billion in September 2025 to $134 billion in February 2026 — driven by the company's successful repositioning from a big data analytics platform into an enterprise AI provider. Databricks has rolled out a series of AI products including Lakebase, Unity, and Omnigent, while becoming a prominent advocate for cost-effective open-weight models, particularly Z.ai's GLM 5.2, which its own internal benchmarking found competitive with proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI at lower cost. The company's trajectory illustrates how enterprise incumbents sitting on large stores of corporate data have been able to capture significant AI investment and valuation multiples without being founded as AI labs.

title: Agility Robotics plants its flag in Tesla’s backyard
summary: Agility Robotics is opening a 60,000-square-foot facility in Fremont, California — near Tesla's Optimus manufacturing site — to train its humanoid robot, Digit, in real-world-like environments. The company already has commercial deployments with customers including Amazon, GXO, Schaeffler, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and has secured $300 million in contract orders. CEO Peggy Johnson is leading Agility through a reverse merger that would make it the first pure-play humanoid robot company on public markets later in 2026. The move signals intensifying competition in the humanoid robotics sector, with Agility positioning its commercial head start against better-capitalized rivals like Tesla.
quote: "We have commercialized. We now know what it takes to walk into these facilities and meet their safety bars, their regulatory bars, compliance, plug into their IT infrastructure, plug into their warehouse management system." — Peggy Johnson, CEO

title: AI-driven memory crunch jolts India’s smartphone market
summary: AI-driven demand for high-bandwidth memory chips is squeezing smartphone makers and consumers in India, where shipments fell 10% year-over-year in Q2 2026 — the steepest June-quarter decline in six years — according to Counterpoint Research. Memory chip manufacturers including Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have shifted production capacity toward the specialized chips used in AI data centers, reducing supply and raising costs for standard consumer devices. India has been hit harder than China because roughly 60% of its smartphone market sits in the sub-₹20,000 segment, where price increases have been most painful, with some models rising as much as 68%. Analysts at both Counterpoint and IDC expect elevated smartphone prices and memory shortages to persist through at least end of 2027, accelerating a shift toward longer upgrade cycles, secondhand devices, and value-over-volume market dynamics.
quote: "For Indian consumers, it is a double whammy as the weaker currency makes imports costlier, which has added to margin pressures for the market players, and they are passing on the cost to the consumer." — Kiranjeet Kaur, Associate Research Director for Mobile Phones Research, IDC

title: TikTok is testing an AI likeness detection tool
summary: TikTok is piloting an opt-in tool that scans for unauthorized AI-generated deepfakes of creators, initially being tested with some US users. Creators must first verify their identity through third-party company Jumio using a real-time selfie scan and ID check, after which TikTok's system searches for AI-generated content potentially using their likeness. Creators can then review findings and report unauthorized posts and accounts to TikTok. The move mirrors a similar tool YouTube recently made available to all adult users, signaling a broader platform push to address AI impersonation concerns.

title: Mila partners with PolArctic to measure sea ice in the High Arctic
summary: Quebec's AI institute Mila has announced a partnership with Halifax-based PolArctic Canada to apply AI expertise to sea-ice monitoring and forecasting in Canada's Arctic waterways. The deal, announced at Mila's 2026 Indigenous AI Gathering, gives PolArctic access to Mila's network of AI researchers and recruitment pipeline for AI talent. PolArctic, a joint venture combining satellite data, ocean science, remote sensing, and traditional Inuit knowledge, serves shipping, fisheries, and northern communities navigating rapid Arctic change. CEO Leslie Canavera framed the partnership as a Canadian sovereignty-building effort, with next-generation forecasting technology aimed at protecting Arctic environments, strengthening supply chains, and empowering Northern communities.

title: How Apple’s big lawsuit could disrupt OpenAI’s IPO plans
summary: Apple filed a trade secrets lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging a pattern of misconduct reaching up to OpenAI's chief hardware officer and noting that more than 400 former Apple employees now work at the company. The lawsuit arrives at a particularly sensitive moment, as OpenAI is reportedly eyeing an IPO as early as later in 2026. The complaint directly threatens OpenAI's hardware ambitions and could complicate its path to going public. The case also raises broader questions about how much users and enterprises should trust AI companies with their data.

title: Apple’s plot to crush OpenAI
summary: Apple has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, and The Vergecast podcast examines whether the legal action reflects genuine competitive concern or an opportunistic strike against a vulnerable rival. The hosts analyze Apple's history of high-profile litigation to assess its strategic motivations, while noting that many legal experts view the specific allegations as standard industry practice. The episode also covers Apple shipping public betas of its new software, including a revamped Siri AI, alongside news of OpenAI gadget leaks, Pixel phone leaks, and OnePlus exiting the US and European markets. The Samsung-Apple duopoly in the US smartphone market appears increasingly entrenched as competitors struggle to gain ground.

title: “We’re counting coupons”: Tech leaders question how foreign investment is shaping domestic innovation
summary: At a MaRS Discovery District panel in Toronto, Canadian tech and academic leaders warned that Canada's approach to foreign AI investment is failing to build genuine domestic capability. Vass Bednar of the Canadian Shield Institute challenged whether commitments like Anthropic's $10-million pledge — delivered largely as Claude credits — or Meta's $13-billion AI data centre plan actually advance Canada's position in the AI value chain, arguing the country needs to own and control tech assets rather than rent them. University of Toronto's Jim Banting added that Canadian graduate talent has few compelling domestic destinations, and that Canada should concentrate funding on select sectors where it can achieve global leadership rather than spreading resources too thin. The discussion came against a backdrop of a 2025 Council of Canadian Academies report finding Canada's science, technology, and innovation performance continues to decline relative to other countries.
quote: "Pick a select number of areas where Canada could have a leadership role, and focus funding programs more deeply on those, versus spreading funding programs across a wide range of things that make it difficult for any one of the groups to get critical mass." — Jim Banting, Assistant Vice-President of Innovation, Partnerships, and Entrepreneurship, University of Toronto

title: San Francisco orders Apple, Google to remove nudify apps from app stores
summary: San Francisco's attorney general David Chiu sent cease-and-desist letters to Apple and Google this week demanding removal of 13 nudification apps from their app stores, citing violations of California laws prohibiting deepfake pornography. The apps, which can strip clothing from photos or place victims in sexualized positions, have victimized primarily women and children at scale; one app alone had over a million downloads. Chiu's office estimates Apple and Google have collectively made millions in fees from these apps, and Google confirmed it suspended the five flagged apps for policy violations, while Apple has not responded. The action also spotlights broader app store enforcement failures, including the ongoing presence of xAI's Grok — which has been used to generate child sexual abuse material — in both stores.
quote: "These images are used to bully, humiliate, and threaten women and girls." — David Chiu, San Francisco Attorney General

title: Patreon stops asking AI bots not to scrape — and starts blocking them
summary: Patreon has moved beyond robots.txt requests to actively blocking AI training crawlers, partnering with Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control technology to prevent unauthorized scraping of creators' content. The shift was prompted by evidence that AI scrapers were ignoring Patreon's existing instructions entirely — during testing, weekly crawling attempts dropped from thousands to zero once active blocking was implemented. The company will still permit indexing bots that direct users back to Patreon, distinguishing between discovery and AI training uses. The move reflects a broader reckoning among online platforms as AI scraping grows more sophisticated and new content features like Patreon's Quips expose more creator work to crawlers.
quote: "Consent shouldn't depend on whether a scraper chooses to behave." — Patreon, Blog Post

title: Apple’s lawsuit couldn’t come at a worse time for OpenAI
summary: Apple filed a trade secrets lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging a pattern of misconduct reaching up to OpenAI's chief hardware officer and noting that more than 400 former Apple employees now work at the company. OpenAI's response has been carefully hedged, and the timing is particularly damaging as the company is reportedly eyeing an IPO as early as later in 2026. The lawsuit directly threatens OpenAI's hardware ambitions at a moment when the company is trying to project stability and growth to potential public market investors. The case also raises broader questions about how much users and enterprises should trust AI companies with sensitive data.

title: Why the first GPU financiers are turning to inference chips in a $400 million deal
summary: General Compute, an AI inference cloud startup, has secured a $400 million loan from Upper90 to purchase SambaNova inference chips — potentially the first financing deal to use inference-specific chips as collateral. Upper90, which pioneered GPU-backed lending with Crusoe in 2021, is betting that demand for cost-efficient AI inference on open-source models will be the next major wave of the AI boom, as frontier model costs drive customers toward cheaper alternatives. The deal signals growing capital market interest in non-Nvidia chip ecosystems, with General Compute claiming its SambaNova SN50 chips deliver 16 times faster inference than GPU-based clouds at lower power and infrastructure costs. The move reflects a broader market shift toward inference infrastructure, as companies like OpenRouter, Fireworks, and chipmakers Groq and Cerebras attract significant investor attention.
quote: "Everyone doesn't need a supercomputer, but they do need inference and AI." — Billy Libby, Co-founder and CEO, Upper90

title: SiftMed lands $5 million to find the facts humans can miss in mountains of medical records
summary: Canadian AI startup SiftMed has raised $5 million CAD in seed funding to expand its AI-powered medical claims document review platform, bringing total funding to nearly $11 million CAD. The St. John's-based company, founded in 2020, uses AI to ingest and analyze thousands of pages of medical records, reducing review time to two hours or less compared to the days it can take human reviewers. The round was led by Toronto's Staircase Ventures with participation from Calgary-based The51 and existing Canadian investors including Pelorus VC and Sandpiper Ventures. Lead investor Janet Bannister cited SiftMed's revenue more than doubling every six months and sees potential for the platform to become part of every medical claim in North America, a market framed as a $26-billion opportunity.
quote: "They are tackling the $26-billion medical claims review process with an AI-based solution that is superior to anything on the market and has strong network effects." — Janet Bannister, Founder and Managing Partner, Staircase Ventures

title: It's official: EU will force Google to share search data and open up AI on Android
summary: The European Commission has finalized binding measures under the Digital Markets Act requiring Google to open Android to competing AI assistants and share search data with rival providers. On Android, Google must allow third-party AI platforms the same deep system integration currently enjoyed by Gemini — including hot-word activation, screen access, and app automation — by July 2027. On search, Google must share data with competing search engines on transparent terms and for a reasonable fee, treating AI chatbots as search services, with compliance required by January 2027. Google has pushed back strongly, arguing the measures threaten user privacy, security, and business trade secrets.
quote: "Today's decisions risk undermining vital privacy and security guardrails for millions of Europeans." — Kent Walker, President of Global Affairs, Google

title: xAI can’t deny Grok makes CSAM anymore. So it’s suing users.
summary: xAI has filed its first lawsuit against a Grok user, targeting Terry Wayne Harwood, who was arrested in South Carolina for using the chatbot to generate child sexual abuse material. The lawsuit is widely seen as a legal strategy to establish that users — not xAI — bear liability for AI-generated illegal content, which could strengthen the company's defense against a looming class action that lawyers estimate could involve thousands of victims. xAI argues that Grok is "a neutral tool, subject to user control" and that all outputs are the responsibility of the user who prompted them. The move comes amid mounting evidence that Grok's safeguards are inadequate, including a 2026 NCMEC report finding that 90 percent of xAI's CyberTipline reports lacked user information actionable by law enforcement.
quote: "Like any generative AI tool, every response, every image, every generation is the result of the user's prompts and directions." — xAI, Complaint

title: Fear of humanoid robots spurs human workers to strike at Hyundai auto factory
summary: Thousands of unionized Hyundai workers at the Ulsan plant in South Korea are staging pre-emptive partial strikes over the automaker's group-wide plan to deploy more than 25,000 Boston Dynamics Atlas humanoid robots across Hyundai and Kia factories — a plan that begins at the non-unionized Metaplant America in Georgia in 2028, not at Ulsan, where no Atlas robot has yet been assigned any task. Workers ended shifts two hours early on July 13-15 and have set four-hour stoppages for July 20-22 after 15 rounds of failed wage talks, demanding fixed monthly salaries to protect against automation-driven hour reductions. It is the auto industry's first factory stoppage tied to humanoid robots, and an early signal of labor resistance to humanoid automation.

title: China’s Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3, the largest open-source model ever, rivaling top U.S. systems
summary: Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based startup backed by Alibaba, has released Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-source model that benchmarks show performing near the top of the market alongside Anthropic's and OpenAI's most powerful proprietary systems. The model's full weights are scheduled for public release on July 27, 2026, making it available for enterprises to fine-tune, self-host, or build upon without API lock-in to Western labs. The release marks a dramatic comeback for Moonshot AI, which had lost significant ground to DeepSeek since early 2025, and represents a strategic bid to become the gravitational center of the global open-source AI developer community. For enterprise leaders, the arrival of a near-frontier open-source model at this scale reshapes the build-versus-buy calculus and signals that the capability gap between open-source and closed proprietary AI has effectively closed.

title: Linus Torvalds to critics of AI coding in Linux: "Fork it. Or just walk away."
summary: Linus Torvalds, creator and top-level maintainer of the Linux kernel, has publicly declared that Linux will not ban AI coding tools and told opponents they are free to fork the project or leave. His statement came amid debate over Sashiko, an agentic AI code review system that its creators say can independently find over half of bugs later fixed by human coders, though with a false positive rate in the 20% range. Torvalds framed his position as one of pragmatic technical merit, saying AI tools have clearly proven their utility and that he will "very loudly ignore" those who argue against others using them. The stance marks a significant signal for the open source community, where tensions between AI tool advocates and anti-AI absolutists have been intensifying.
quote: "Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects, and if somebody has issues with that, they can do the open-source thing and fork it. Or just walk away." — Linus Torvalds, Linux kernel creator and maintainer

title: Google Vids now lets you star in your own AI videos
summary: Google is expanding its Vids platform to allow users to create personalized AI avatars based on a selfie and voice recording, pushing the workplace presentation tool toward a broader AI video creation platform. The update also brings Gemini Omni to Vids, enabling video generation from written prompts and reference images, along with editing capabilities such as background swapping, lighting correction, and step-by-step iterative edits. The move puts Google in more direct competition with AI video startups like HeyGen, Synthesia, and D-ID. Avatars will be watermarked with Google's SynthID technology, tied to users' Google accounts, and restricted to users aged 18 or older in eligible regions.

title: Roblox launches an AI-powered game-creation feature in its mobile app
summary: Roblox is launching a feature called Build that lets users create games on mobile devices using AI, converting simple text prompts into playable games without any programming experience. The feature will enter public alpha testing on July 28, initially available to users in New Zealand aged nine and older, with those 16 and up able to publish games globally. The launch comes amid broader industry concern about AI-generated content flooding platforms — a 2026 GDC survey found 52% of game industry professionals believe generative AI is negatively impacting the industry. Roblox says it will address quality concerns by ranking AI-generated games on player retention, ensuring low-engagement titles receive less visibility.
quote: "Our discovery systems are designed to highlight games with long-term retention, which doesn't include AI slop." — Roblox, Company Statement

title: New York governor says she’s using AI to analyze ‘every single rule’ in the state
summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that her administration is using AI to review every rule, regulation, and policy in the state, uncovering outdated laws such as a $25 fee to take a dog hunting and a requirement for pregnant workers to obtain a permit to work after midnight. A review that Hochul estimated would have taken five years at the staff level was completed in a couple of months using AI. The effort is intended to allow the governor and state agencies to eliminate obsolete regulations. The announcement comes even as New York became the first state to impose a moratorium of up to one year on new hyperscale data centers.
quote: "I want a government that's not on your back but on your side, and using AI has been powerful to do that." — Kathy Hochul, Governor of New York

title: Google is renaming NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook
summary: Google is rebranding its AI note-taking app NotebookLM as Gemini Notebook, deepening its integration across the Gemini ecosystem and Google Search while keeping it a standalone app. The renamed product will soon be accessible through AI Mode, Google's chatbot-like experience in Search. Alongside the rebrand, Google is rolling out an update enabling Gemini Notebook to connect to a secure cloud computer to write and execute code, currently available to AI Ultra and Workspace business customers with Pro users on web to follow in coming weeks. The move signals Google's broader strategy of consolidating its AI tools under the Gemini brand while expanding their reach into core products like Search.

title: Google’s AI Mode now lets you link and interact with select apps
summary: Google has expanded AI Mode, its conversational search experience, to support direct integration with third-party apps including Instacart, Canva, and YouTube Music, allowing users to complete tasks — such as adding groceries to a cart or saving a playlist — without leaving the AI interface. The move positions AI Mode as a task-completion platform rather than just a question-answering tool. Google explicitly aims to compete with OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude, both of which already support app integrations. The rollout is live in the U.S., with more app partnerships planned.

title: How a former DeepMind researcher raised at a $300M pre-seed valuation before launching a product
summary: Andrew Dai, a former Google DeepMind researcher whose work helped inform ChatGPT, has raised a $55 million seed round for his new AI startup Elorian at a $300 million valuation — before launching any product. Elorian is focused on visual AI and visual reasoning, an area Dai argues has seen far less progress than domains like coding or mathematics. The valuation-to-capital ratio is notably more aggressive than that of Thinking Machines, which recently closed one of the largest AI funding rounds in U.S. history. Dai chose strategic investors including Nvidia and Menlo Ventures over higher-valuation offers, prioritizing partners who understood the realities of building frontier AI.
quote: "One area where progress has been extremely uneven is visual understanding and visual reasoning." — Andrew Dai, Founder and CEO, Elorian

title: Why AMI Labs’ Alexandre LeBrun won’t call his AI ‘AGI’ or ‘superintelligence’
summary: AMI Labs, the world model startup co-founded by Turing Award winner Yann LeCun after he left Meta, is positioning itself at the intersection of physical AI and robotics, with CEO Alexandre LeBrun rejecting industry buzzwords like "AGI" and "superintelligence" as lacking meaningful definition. The company, which raised $1.03 billion in March 2026 at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation, has no product yet but is actively courting industrial partners in robotics, manufacturing, and electronics. LeBrun argues that large language models remain weak in physical environments and that world models — which predict the next state of the real world rather than the next word — are needed to give robots genuine situational awareness and safety. The startup is targeting Asia, and South Korea in particular, for its combination of advanced hardware industries and rapid technology adoption.
quote: "The hardware is very advanced; progress in hardware in the last few months is incredible, but there's no brain." — Alexandre LeBrun, CEO, AMI Labs

title: Moonshot’s upcoming Kimi 3 is expected to close the gap with Anthropic’s Opus 4.8
summary: Moonshot AI's forthcoming Kimi K3 model is expected to match or surpass Anthropic's Opus 4.8, according to the Financial Times, citing anonymous sources. The model will reportedly be the largest open-weight AI model from China, with a parameter count between 2 and 3 trillion, and is set to release within days. The development signals a continued narrowing of the capability gap between Chinese open-source models and leading closed-source Western frontier models, intensifying the debate over whether enterprises should pay for expensive proprietary AI. Moonshot is also said to be raising fresh capital at a $31.5 billion valuation, up sharply from its $20 billion valuation in a May 2026 funding round.

title: Apple Intelligence approved for launch in China with Alibaba and Baidu
summary: China's internet regulator, the Cyberspace Administration of China, has approved Apple Intelligence for launch in the country, with Alibaba's Qwen AI models to be integrated into Apple's operating systems including iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS. Baidu has also confirmed a partnership with Apple to develop Apple Intelligence features for Chinese users, and Apple is said to be exploring further integrations with DeepSeek and ByteDance. The approvals end a regulatory delay that had kept Apple Intelligence — launched in 2024 — out of the Chinese market. The development is strategically significant: Greater China generated $20.5 billion in Apple sales in Q2 2026, up 28% year-over-year, and Apple recently reclaimed the No. 2 spot in China's smartphone market.

title: Claude can now use your 1Password credentials for you
summary: 1Password has launched a browser integration that allows Anthropic's Claude to access stored login credentials — such as usernames, passwords, and MFA codes — to complete multi-step agentic tasks like booking travel or managing online accounts without user interruption. The feature uses a "zero-exposure security framework" that injects credentials through a secure channel Claude cannot view, meaning the AI can use but never actually see passwords or one-time codes. Users must approve each credential request via a biometric prompt, and 1Password automatically locks the vault to only the credentials explicitly granted for the current task. The integration is available now for 1Password users on Mac across business, family, and individual plans, with support for payment cards and identity details planned for a later release.
quote: "The moment an AI agent takes control of the browser, 1Password locks down automatically, limiting access to only the credentials explicitly granted for the current task." — 1Password, Company Statement

title: Google ordered to open Android and Search to rivals in Europe
summary: The European Union has ordered Google to give rival AI assistants and search engines comparable access to Android and Google Search data under the Digital Markets Act, with deadlines of January 2027 for search data sharing and July 2027 for Android changes. The Android ruling would allow competing AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity to be as deeply integrated into Android devices as Google's own Gemini, including access to voice commands, app interactions, and device hardware. The Search ruling requires Google to share data generated by its search engine with competing search engines and AI chatbots. Non-compliance could trigger fines of up to 10 percent of Google's global annual turnover, potentially tens of billions of dollars.
quote: "With today's measures, we want to support innovation and diversity in the European Union, enabling fair competition in the markets of AI assistant for Android devices and search engines." — Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice President for Tech Sovereignty, Security, and Democracy, European Commission

title: Computer cops
summary: AI companies are aggressively selling law enforcement agencies a new generation of tools — including real-time crime centers, facial recognition, automated report-writing, drones, and AI chatbots — that collectively aim to automate core policing decisions. Companies like Axon Enterprise and Motorola Solutions are competing to own the entire police technology stack, from data collection to AI-driven operational decision-making, with Axon reporting 700 percent year-over-year growth in AI product revenue and a 140 percent surge in its AI Era Plan subscriptions. Critics, including legal scholars and even some police officials, warn that embedding opaque algorithms into law enforcement will deepen accountability gaps and that past "data-driven" policing tools failed to prevent violent incidents. The article, reported by The Verge's Webb Wright from the IACP Technology Conference in Fort Worth, Texas, highlights how the absence of federal oversight leaves departments largely reliant on vendors' own claims about safety and effectiveness.
quote: "We are determined to become the AI company in public safety, and we are well on our way." — Joshua Isner, President, Axon

title: GroundedAI secures $2 million to help modernize tunnel building
summary: Canadian startup GroundedAI has raised $2 million CAD in a round led by StandUp Ventures, bringing its total equity funding to $2.8 million, to expand its AI-powered software for underground construction projects. The Vancouver company sells a platform that helps engineers, geologists, and project managers digitally capture and analyze subsurface ground conditions in real time, with AI assistance, replacing fragmented methods like paper sketches, spreadsheets, and mobile phone photos. The funding comes as Canada, under Prime Minister Mark Carney, pushes to accelerate major infrastructure development including transit, hydro, pipelines, and mines — sectors where tunnelling is essential. CEO Shelby Yee points to cost-overrun disasters like the Eglinton Crosstown LRT as evidence that poor real-time ground data is a core, underappreciated driver of project failures.
quote: "Transit expansion, pumped hydro, power transmission, water and wastewater systems, gas pipelines, and the mines supplying the critical minerals for all of it all require tunnelling or underground construction." — Shelby Yee, Co-founder and CEO, GroundedAI

title: Applied Computing wants to give oil and gas operators an AI model for the entire plant
summary: Applied Computing, a London-based startup founded in 2023, has raised a $20 million Series A led by engineering firm KBR, with Databricks Ventures participating, to expand its foundation AI model for the oil, gas, refining, and petrochemical industries. The company's model, Orbital, combines time series, physics-based, and language models to analyze sensor data, engineering documentation, and physics in real time, enabling operators to detect anomalies and run simulations within minutes rather than days or weeks. Applied Computing claims to have reached double-digit millions in annual recurring revenue within 18 months of emerging from stealth, with customers including large upstream and downstream energy companies, and partners such as Wipro and KBR, which has integrated Orbital into its INSITE 3.0 platform. The funding will support international expansion, including a new Houston office, additional hires, and planned moves into the Middle East.
quote: "It's getting those three data sources to talk to each other in real time. That's the real key." — Callum Adamson, Co-founder and CEO, Applied Computing

title: Microsoft is reportedly training salespeople to talk down OpenAI and Anthropic
summary: Microsoft is coaching its sales team to negatively compare AI products from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic to its own, according to Bloomberg, as part of a strategy session for the new fiscal year. Executives emphasized pitching Microsoft's in-house models as a more efficient and cost-effective end-to-end system, with one executive directly comparing Copilot to Anthropic's Claude and claiming Claude is slower, less accurate, and lacks proper security integrations within Microsoft's office apps. The move reflects a broader strategic shift: Microsoft has been quietly replacing OpenAI and Anthropic models in flagship products like Word and Excel with its own, and the two companies amended their partnership in April to drop exclusivity. The competitive posturing comes as Microsoft faces investor skepticism over its massive AI spending and seeks to demonstrate that its in-house AI capabilities can stand on their own.
quote: "Everyone else is selling parts — we're selling the full end-to-end system. That's the story that we all need to get out there and tell in FY27." — Jay Parikh, Executive Vice President, Microsoft

title: xAI sues a man for using Grok to generate CSAM ‘deepfakes’
summary: xAI has filed a lawsuit against South Carolina man Terry Wayne Harwood, who was arrested in February and faces eight felony charges for allegedly possessing and distributing child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The company claims Harwood bypassed Grok's safeguards to generate and distribute CSAM, including converting non-sexual photographs of minors into sexually explicit images. xAI argues the conduct exposed it to significant legal and reputational damage, and is seeking compensation for any costs incurred defending itself against victims' legal actions. The suit marks the first time xAI has taken legal action over deepfakes created with Grok, following earlier controversy over the platform's image-editing features generating sexualized images of minors.
quote: "Anyone using Grok to make illegal content will suffer the same consequences as if they upload illegal content." — Elon Musk, CEO, xAI

title: Which LLMs are secretly Canadian?
summary: Anthropic announced a $10 million CAD investment in Canadian research, but critics note the funds are offered as Claude API credits rather than cash, raising questions about whether the initiative builds Canadian AI capacity or simply locks institutions into Anthropic's products. Separately, a study by Transformer Labs found that leading LLMs — despite being built and trained in the US — produce outputs that align more closely with Canadian cultural values than American ones, described as the unintended result of training models to be polite, tolerant, and institutionally deferential. Richard Sutton, one of the early Canadian AI researchers Anthropic cited as justification for its investment, launched a new Canadian research lab aimed at developing artificial general intelligence that runs on the power of a few lightbulbs. The contrast highlights a broader strategic question for Canada: whether its AI policy is cultivating homegrown innovation or producing well-funded users of foreign platforms.

title: Amazon AGI director says AI agent reliability, not capability, is blocking enterprise deployment at VB Transform 2026
summary: Bryan Silverthorn, Director of AGI Autonomy at Amazon, told VB Transform 2026 that the central obstacle to enterprise AI agent deployment is reliability, not capability — framing it across four dimensions: consistency, robustness, predictability, and safety. He described a real customer case where an agent worked flawlessly for two months before intermittently misreading serial numbers due to a vision encoder sensitivity triggered by an imperceptible software change, illustrating how agents that pass internal evals routinely fail in production. VentureBeat research reinforces the scale of the problem: half of surveyed companies shipped agents that passed internal tests but failed real customers, and most enterprises track uptime while ignoring accuracy. Silverthorn's prescription is largely cultural — treating agents like interns who need active management, risk assessment, and undo capabilities rather than just better models.
quote: "The models have to be better. Obviously, we're working hard on making the models better." — Bryan Silverthorn, Director of AGI Autonomy, Amazon

title: Siemens Canada to expand Saskatoon R&D hub by 10,000 square feet
summary: Siemens Canada is expanding its research and development hub in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan by 10,000 square feet, bringing its total footprint at the Innovation Saskatchewan Research and Technology Park to roughly 45,000 square feet. The expansion, focused on AI-powered electronic design automation (EDA) software for semiconductor chip design, is expected to add up to 100 high-skill roles over the next two years, growing the facility's workforce to approximately 400 employees. The move signals growing investment in Canadian semiconductor and industrial AI capability at a time when Canada remains the only G7 nation without a standalone semiconductor strategy. Siemens Canada's choice of Saskatoon reflects the city's deep-tech talent pipeline and a longstanding partnership with the University of Saskatchewan, where the company funds an EDA Chair position.
quote: "Siemens is expanding a world-class team developing AI-powered software and advanced engineering technologies to help semiconductor companies design, validate, and bring increasingly complex chips to market." — Faisal Kazi, President and CEO, Siemens Canada

title: Amid hardware legal battle, OpenAI releases a $230 keyboard for Codex
summary: OpenAI has entered the hardware market with the Codex Micro, a $230 light-up keyboard co-designed with Work Louder, built to help users manage AI coding agents through physical controls including agent status keys, customizable shortcuts, and a reasoning-level dial. The device is a limited-run item and connects to the ChatGPT desktop app, positioning it more as a novelty than a mass-market product. More consequentially, Bloomberg revealed a separate screenless, portable smart speaker with moving parts still in development, reportedly designed by former Apple engineers. That connection has fueled a lawsuit from Apple, which is accusing OpenAI's senior leadership of deliberately extracting and using Apple's confidential information in developing its own hardware — a charge OpenAI denies.

title: SpaceX falls to $135 IPO price ahead of Starship launch
summary: SpaceX shares fell back to their $135 IPO price on July 15, 2026, briefly dipping below $133 before closing at $135.27 — a sharp decline from the post-IPO high of over $200 reached in the weeks following the company's June 12 public listing, which raised nearly $86 billion. The stock's volatility is partly attributed to a small float of just 4% of total shares trading on Nasdaq, combined with intense market scrutiny. SpaceX's stock performance is being watched closely because it signals investor confidence in Elon Musk's broader vision, and is seen as a bellwether for upcoming IPOs by AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have filed confidential IPO registrations. The company faces an additional test Thursday with a Starship rocket launch — its first since the IPO — which will end in planned splashdowns in the Gulf of Mexico regardless of success.

title: Thinking Machines amps up its bet against one-size-fits-all AI with its first open model, Inkling
summary: Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its first AI model, Inkling — an open-weight, mixture-of-experts system with 975 billion total parameters trained on 45 trillion tokens across text, image, audio, and video. The company explicitly acknowledges Inkling is not the strongest model available, positioning it instead as a customizable starting point for enterprises to fine-tune through its Tinker platform, betting that organization-specific AI will outperform general-purpose models. The release arrives amid growing momentum for open and private AI alternatives, with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warning that enterprises using proprietary models effectively "pay twice" and Hugging Face's CEO predicting frontier models will increasingly be reserved for high-value tasks. Thinking Machines claims it reached this milestone in roughly nine months, compared to the three-to-five years it took OpenAI and Anthropic, though its funding situation and path to revenue remain unclear.
quote: "Frontier models will increasingly be reserved for experimentation and high-value tasks, while most production AI work shifts to private or open-source alternatives."

title: Suno snatched millions of songs from YouTube, Genius, and Deezer
summary: Hacked files obtained from AI music generator Suno reveal that the company scraped millions of songs and lyrics from YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius, and other platforms to train its AI models, according to 404 Media. The leaked source code from 2023 and 2024 includes scraping instructions targeting multiple platforms and indicates Suno consumed over two million YouTube Music clips, alongside hundreds of thousands of hours of audio from other services. The disclosure is significant because Suno faces multiple lawsuits, including one from the RIAA, which alleges Suno unlawfully circumvented YouTube's copyright protections through "stream ripping" — claims the leaked data appears to support. Suno's customer data, including email addresses and payment details, was also accessed in the breach, which the company says it discovered in November 2025 but did not disclose to affected users.

title: Hack suggests AI music generator Suno scraped YouTube for training data
summary: A hacker who breached AI music generator Suno in November 2025 accessed source code allegedly revealing that the company systematically scraped audio from YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius, stock music libraries, and podcast RSS feeds for AI training data. Suno had previously acknowledged training on publicly available internet content, claiming fair use protections, but major record labels suing the company argue that circumventing YouTube's scraping protections violates the DMCA. The breach also exposed customer data including emails, phone numbers, and partial credit card numbers, yet Suno did not notify affected customers and described it as a limited, quickly contained incident. The revelations intensify ongoing legal pressure on AI music generators, with competitor Udio facing similar YouTube scraping allegations.

title: Microsoft patches record number of security vulnerabilities, citing its use of AI
summary: Microsoft issued patches for 570 security flaws on Tuesday as part of its monthly Patch Tuesday release, a record number the company attributes to its use of AI in uncovering previously hidden code vulnerabilities. At least two of the flaws are zero-days being actively exploited: one allows privilege escalation on Windows Server, and another affects SharePoint, which CISA has warned is being actively targeted by hackers. Microsoft's Windows chief signaled this elevated volume will become the new normal as AI models grow more capable at finding dormant bugs, including in legacy Windows code dating back decades.
